model.description: Positive integers a_1,...,a_n and nonnegative target t, n>=2; repeats and empty subset allowed. Let b be maximum input/target bit length. Word RAM has w=ceil(4(n+b+log2(n+2))) bits. Reads/writes, indirect addressing, comparison, arithmetic including multiply/divide/remainder, bitwise operations and shifts cost one word operation; overflow uses charged multiple operations. Independent uniform w-bit random word costs one operation; one-way randomness with retained words charged to memory. One finite program for all n,b, no advice or external tables; all preprocessing and input access charged. Halts on every run, correct with probability at least 2/3 for every fixed input. For every fixed c and b<=n^c, every random outcome costs O(2^(0.49n)); program does not depend on c.

score.definition: Worst-case over random outcomes O(2^(alpha n)), for each fixed polynomial input-bit bound b<=n^c; per-input success probability at least 2/3.

li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.proof_status: Written proof in an arXiv preprint; no Lean proof. The paper counts bit operations on inputs of up to 2^(o(n)) bits and says its algorithm is uniform (v2). No Big O Speedrun proof check. Evidence remains Claimed.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.comparison_status: Theorem 4.1 of v1: a randomized algorithm in O(2^(0.4999977...n)) = O(2^((1/2 - 1/450000)n)) bit operations in the worst case; if a solution exists it returns one with probability at least 99 percent, otherwise it returns the failure symbol, and it never returns an incorrect solution. Comparison with the board model, a word RAM with b <= n^c: a bound in bit operations gives the same bound in word operations, because one bit operation costs at most one word operation; the paper allows integers in Z and input length up to 2^(o(n)) bits (v2, Section 2), a wider class than positive integers with b <= n^c; the 99 percent success is at least 2/3, and the time bound is for the worst case. The paper says the algorithm is uniform: the circuits are constructed explicitly for every n (v2, Section 1, Uniformization), and its hash function handles input integers of up to 2^(o(n)) bits (v2, footnote 3). v1 Theorem 1.1 states 0.499999 and Theorem 4.1 states 1/2 - 1/450000; v2 states 0.49999777... in both. Source comparison, not a proof check.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.scope: Randomized algorithm for Subset Sum with integers in Z and a target in Z, worst case over random outcomes, success probability at least 99 percent, measured in bit operations on inputs of up to 2^(o(n)) bits.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.exact_statement: Subset sum can be solved by a randomized algorithm in O(2^((1/2 - 1/450000)n)) bit operations in the worst case; if a solution exists it is returned with probability at least 99 percent, and no incorrect solution is returned.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.score_interpretation: Attained exponent 1/2 - 1/450000 = 0.49999777...; the paper proves O(2^((1/2 - xi/9 + epsilon)n)) for every epsilon > 0 with xi > 1/50000 and states the exponent 1/2 - 1/450000 in Theorem 4.1.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.license_status: arXiv non-exclusive license; the paper is not copied, only its hash
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.credits: Baitian Li and Lixi Ye. Builds on the representation technique of Randolph and Wegrzycki (STOC 2026) and the depth-2 linear circuit framework of Alman and Li (FOCS 2025). The paper's AI disclosure credits GPT-6 Pro and GPT-6 Astra for parts of the work.
li-ye-subset-sum-0-4999978-2026.credit_note: Baitian Li and Lixi Ye take the exponent of Subset Sum below 1/2 with the representation technique of Randolph and Węgrzycki, where testing two partial solutions is the partial match problem, and a depth 2 linear circuit for it, following Alman and Li. The paper says it was developed independently of OpenAI's 0.49 paper. Its AI disclosure says GPT-6 Pro built the first circuit and GPT-6 Astra found the reduction for ordinary subset sum.
